section_summaries.epidemiology: Acute respiratory illnesses (ARIs) are the most frequent illnesses globally, often limited to the upper airways and self-limiting, but can progress to lower respiratory tract infections (LRTIs) like bronchiolitis and pneumonia. Children and elderly, especially in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), are at increased risk. Childhood pneumonia is a leading cause of mortality in children under 5, accounting for 16% of all deaths in this age group in 2015. Pneumonia also causes significant morbidity and mortality in older adults. Most respiratory viruses spread person-to-person via respiratory routes (large droplets, small aerosols, fomites) with hand contamination. Patients are most infectious early in disease. Children play a major role in community outbreaks. Handwashing and covering coughs/sneezes can partially prevent transmission. Many viruses show seasonal variation, with influenza and RSV epidemics in winter in temperate regions, while tropical patterns are less clear, with peaks coinciding with lower temperatures, humidity, or rainfall.
section_summaries.pathogenesis: Acute RTIs typically begin in the upper respiratory tract (nose, mouth, eyes) and spread to lower airways within 2-4 days. Clinical syndromes overlap, presenting with fever, cough, and malaise, caused by various pathogens. Common cold symptoms result from local infection of ciliated nasal mucosal epithelium cells and increased vascular permeability. Pharyngitis pain is caused by chemical inflammation mediators. Croup symptoms stem from localized subglottic inflammation and edema. Tracheitis and tracheobronchitis are due to tracheal and bronchial epithelium infection. Bronchiolitis involves direct viral infection of bronchiolar epithelial cells, leading to increased mucus secretion and dense debris plugs, impeding expiratory airflow. Primary viral pneumonia is characterized by dysfunctional gas exchange and lung parenchyma inflammation, with viruses reaching small airways via continuous spread or aerosol inhalation. Mucosal infection causes epithelial cell destruction, hyperemia, edema, hemorrhaging, and cellular infiltration, compromising respiratory function. RSV and hMPV cause severe disease in the first year of life, and reinfections are common in elderly and immunocompromised patients.
section_summaries.clinical_manifestations: Viral respiratory infections range from common cold to severe lower respiratory tract infections with systemic dissemination. Severe disease can affect all age groups, but young children, the elderly, and the immunocompromised are at higher risk. The common cold (coryza) presents with runny or stuffed nose, sneezing, and sore throat. Pharyngitis involves sore throat. Croup, common in children under 3, is characterized by a barking cough and acute inspiratory stridor. Tracheitis and tracheobronchitis cause tracheal tenderness, substernal discomfort on inhalation, and non-productive cough. Bronchiolitis, a distinct syndrome in infants, manifests with wheezing, flaring nostrils, use of accessory respiratory muscles, and cyanosis in severe cases. Viral pneumonia involves acute generalized illness, dry cough, rhinitis, conjunctivitis, increased respiratory rate, and cyanosis in very severe disease, with radiographic changes indicating lung inflammation. Secondary bacterial pneumonia may follow viral illness, presenting with recurrent or protracted fever and respiratory symptoms.
section_summaries.diagnosis: Clinical history and examination offer clues but are non-specific due to overlapping syndromes. Etiologic diagnosis requires detection of virus, antigens, or nucleic acids in respiratory/other specimens, or retrospectively by immune response in paired serum samples. Rapid antigen tests for RSV and influenza are available but have limited sensitivity (up to 70%). Molecular identification of a single viral agent does not exclude co-infections. Biomarkers like C-reactive protein, procalcitonin, and Mx A are investigated to differentiate bacterial vs. viral infections and reduce unnecessary antibiotic use.
section_summaries.treatment: Treatment for mild respiratory infections is often self-limiting, as seen with the common cold. For influenza, neuraminidase inhibitors (oseltamivir, zanamivir, peramivir, laninamivir) are effective if administered within 48 hours of symptom onset, primarily for severe cases. Convalescent plasma, human immunoglobulin, and other immunomodulatory approaches are under investigation for severe influenza. Antibiotics are often inappropriately used for viral RTIs, especially in LMICs, leading to concerns about resistance; their use should be discouraged for mild viral illnesses. No specific antiviral treatments are widely available for other common respiratory viruses besides influenza.
section_summaries.prevention: Prevention includes frequent handwashing and covering the mouth during coughing or sneezing. Efficacious vaccines are available for influenza virus, Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae. Annual influenza vaccination is recommended, with vaccine formulations updated twice yearly for dominant strains. A live oral adenovirus serotype 4 and 7 vaccine is used for military recruits in the USA. Vaccines for other respiratory viruses like RSV are not widely available, and some past RSV vaccine attempts were associated with more severe disease. Antimeiotics (amantadine and rimantadine) were formerly used for influenza prevention but are now considered outmoded. Control of MERS coronavirus is difficult due to its natural reservoir and asymptomatic human spreaders, though vaccination of dromedary camels is proposed. Continuous monitoring and surveillance of novel avian influenza viruses in poultry and wild birds are crucial due to pandemic potential.
